title: Choosing the right method
blurb: Weigh face-to-face, physical and virtual methods against each other and pick the right one for the message and the audience.
question: A leisure centre refurbishment must announce a road closure to elderly neighbours, agree a design change with the client and give a weekly update to contractors on three sites. Which method suits each message, and why?

teach.h: No method is best for everything
teach.body: Each method has advantages and disadvantages, so the project manager matches the method to the MESSAGE (how sensitive, complex, formal or urgent it is) and to the AUDIENCE (how many people, where they are, what technology they have, what they prefer). Often the best answer is a blend: discuss in one method, confirm in another. Choosing well is what makes the meaning received match the meaning sent.

teach.h: The three methods side by side
What does the message need most?
teach.caption: Then check the audience: can they actually receive it that way?

items: Who is the audience, how many are there, and where are they?
How sensitive or complex is the message? Will there be questions or emotion?
Do we need a formal, lasting record?
What technology and skills does the audience have?
Do we need feedback straight away?

teach.h: Scenario: the Seaview Leisure Centre refurbishment
teach.body: Jamal holds the kick-off face to face to build trust with the client. Many neighbours are elderly and offline, so road closures go out as printed letters and on the library notice board. Contractors on three sites join a weekly video call and use a shared tool between calls. When the client and Jamal agree a design change in person, he confirms it by email the same day and it goes through change control in writing.

teach.caption: Each method covers another's weakness: the meeting has no record, the email has no body language, the document is slow.

teach.h: Face to face vs video call
teach.caption: A video call is the closest virtual method to face to face, but it is still virtual.

teach.text: The exam names ONE method and offers advantages or disadvantages that belong to ANOTHER. Before you answer, ask: does this option really belong to the method in the stem? 'Permanent record' is physical, 'richest cues' is face to face, 'depends on technology' is virtual.

items: Match the method to the message (sensitivity, complexity, formality, urgency) and the audience (size, location, technology, preference).
Face to face: sensitive or complex. Physical: formal and lasting. Virtual: fast, wide, routine.
Blend methods so one covers another's weakness (meet, then confirm in writing).
Check every option belongs to the method named in the question.

summary: You can now compare face-to-face, physical and virtual communication on feedback, cues, record, reach, cost and technology, and choose the right method, or blend of methods, for a given message and audience.

A.q: Which method is the best choice for telling a key supplier that a phase of work has been cancelled?
options: A printed notice on the board
A face-to-face meeting
An item in the newsletter
A message in the team chat
A.why: Cancellation is sensitive and will raise questions and emotion, so face to face, with empathy and immediate feedback, suits it best (with written confirmation after).

whyNot.0: A public notice is impersonal and gives no chance to respond.
whyNot.2: A newsletter is slow, public and one-way for sensitive news.
whyNot.3: A chat message lacks the cues and care this news needs.

A.q: Which pairing of method and advantage is correct?
options: Virtual: the richest non-verbal cues
Face to face: an automatic audit trail
Physical: a permanent, lasting record
Physical: instant two-way feedback
A.why: Printed and tangible communication lasts and can be filed, giving a permanent record.

whyNot.0: Virtual methods give fewer cues; the richest are face to face.
whyNot.1: Face to face leaves no record unless minutes are taken.
whyNot.3: Physical communication is one-way when read; no instant feedback.

A.q: A team spread across four countries needs a short status update today. Which method is most suitable?
options: A face-to-face meeting
A posted printed report
A site notice board
An email or video call
A.why: Virtual methods reach dispersed people quickly and cheaply, which is what a same-day update to four countries needs.

whyNot.0: Gathering four countries in person today is impractical and costly.
whyNot.1: Posting a report abroad would take days.
whyNot.2: A notice board only reaches people at that site.

B.q: Which pairing of method and disadvantage is correct?
options: Virtual: it depends on technology
Face to face: no immediate feedback
Physical: it needs internet access
Virtual: travel costs are high
B.why: Virtual communication relies on working technology, plus access and skills to use it.

whyNot.1: Immediate feedback is a face-to-face advantage.

B.q: Why might a project manager deliver the same important message through more than one method?
options: It doubles the length of every message
It removes the need for any feedback
One method covers another's weakness
It means no record needs to be kept
B.why: Blending methods (for example, discuss in person then confirm by email) lets the strengths of one offset the weaknesses of another.

whyNot.0: The aim is clarity and coverage, not longer messages.
whyNot.1: Feedback is still needed to confirm understanding.
whyNot.3: Blending often adds a record rather than removing one.

B.q: What should mainly drive a project manager's choice of communication method?
options: The method used on the last project
The message and the audience's needs
The project manager's own preference
Whichever method costs the least
B.why: The right method depends on what the message is (sensitive, formal, urgent) and who must receive it (number, location, access, preference).

whyNot.0: Each project's stakeholders differ; copying past choices may not fit.
whyNot.2: Personal preference ignores what the audience needs.
whyNot.3: The cheapest method may fail to get the meaning across.

C.q: A leisure centre project must tell nearby residents, many elderly and offline, about road closure dates. Which method is most suitable?
options: A post on the project's social media
A group email to the residents' list
A printed letter to each household
A live webinar on the closure plan
C.why: A printed letter reaches people without internet access and gives them a lasting record of the dates.

whyNot.0: Offline residents would not see social media posts.
whyNot.1: Many residents have no email, so they would be missed.
whyNot.3: A webinar needs devices and skills many residents lack.

C.q: Which TWO are advantages of virtual over physical communication? 1) Faster to send. 2) Easier to update. 3) Does not depend on technology. 4) Can never be misread.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
C.why: Virtual messages go out instantly and can be corrected or reissued quickly, whereas printed material is slow and goes out of date.

whyNot.1: Statement 3 is wrong: virtual communication does depend on technology.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: virtual messages are often misread because cues are missing.
whyNot.3: Both are wrong: virtual needs technology, and any written message can be misread.

C.q: A sponsor proposes moving a contentious scope workshop from the boardroom to a video call to save travel. What is the main communication disadvantage of this change?
options: No one could take part from other sites
Fewer non-verbal cues would be picked up
The workshop would cost more to run
No decisions could be recorded at all
C.why: A video call gives fewer non-verbal cues than meeting in person, which matters most in a contentious discussion where reactions need reading.

whyNot.0: A video call lets people join from other sites; that is its advantage.
whyNot.2: A video call removes travel, so it usually costs less.
whyNot.3: Decisions can still be minuted, or the call recorded.

reteach.title: Organising a music festival
reteach.question: A festival organiser has to deal with headline acts, thousands of ticket holders and the local council. Would one method of communication suit them all?

blocks.body: The headline act's fee is negotiated over dinner: face to face, because it is sensitive and needs give and take. The council licence conditions arrive as a signed, printed document: physical, because it must be formal and lasting. Thousands of ticket holders get the stage times by app notification and email: virtual, because it must be fast and reach everyone. Same organiser, three methods, each chosen for its message and audience.

blocks.text: If the organiser emailed the headline act a take-it-or-leave-it fee, or posted letters to 20,000 ticket holders, each method's weakness would show. The wrong method is a communication failure.

explain.body: Ask how sensitive, complex, formal and urgent the message is. Sensitive or complex topics need face to face. Formal content that must be kept needs a physical (or written) record. Urgent, simple updates suit virtual.

test.q: Which message most needs a method that allows immediate two-way discussion?
options: The dial-in details for a weekly call
Negotiating a revised delivery date
The standard site opening times
A reminder that timesheets are due
test.why: Negotiation is complex and needs back-and-forth, so it calls for a method with immediate feedback, ideally face to face.

whyNot.0: Dial-in details are simple facts that suit a message or email.
whyNot.2: Standing information suits a notice or the intranet.
whyNot.3: A routine reminder suits a quick virtual message.

explain.body: How many people, where are they, what technology and skills do they have, and what do they prefer? Dispersed audiences point to virtual. Offline audiences point to physical. Small, local groups dealing with a hard topic point to face to face.

test.q: Which audience feature most strongly points towards a virtual method?
options: Members who have no internet access
Members who need a signed record
Members spread across several countries
Members all based in one site office
test.why: Virtual methods reach dispersed people quickly and cheaply, so an audience in several countries points that way.

whyNot.0: No internet access rules virtual methods out; physical suits them.
whyNot.1: A signed record points to a physical document.
whyNot.3: A co-located group can easily meet face to face.

explain.body: Face to face: richest cues and immediate feedback. Physical: a lasting, tangible record. Virtual: speed and reach at low cost. When a question names a strength, match it to its owner.

items.label: Face to face: words, tone and body language
Virtual: fast, wide and low cost

test.q: Which method's signature strength is a tangible, permanent record?
options: Face to face
Virtual
Telephone
Physical
test.why: Physical communication (printed reports, letters, signed documents) is tangible and lasting.

whyNot.0: Face to face leaves no record unless minutes are taken.
whyNot.1: Written virtual tools can keep records, but tangibility is the physical hallmark.
whyNot.2: A phone call is virtual and usually leaves no record.

explain.body: Use a second method to cover the first one's weakness. Discuss face to face, then confirm by email for a record. Send a report, then hold a call to answer questions. Post a notice, then email remote staff who will not see it.

test.q: After agreeing actions in a face-to-face meeting, why should the project manager send an email summary?
options: To create a record of what was agreed
To replace the need for the meeting
To add body language to the decisions
To avoid anyone asking any questions
test.why: Face to face leaves no automatic record; a written summary captures the decisions and actions so they are not disputed later.

whyNot.1: The meeting has already done its job of discussion; the email complements it.
whyNot.3: Questions are welcome; feedback confirms understanding.
